note: HL05 chapter capability ledger. Authored intent, not a derived cache: no validator may rewrite this file. All 41 Latin chapters are authored here. Chapters 1, 19, 21, 33 and 36 own a terminal consolidation lesson that recombines the chapter's material; every other chapter's payoff is still its last lesson by sequence, which is where that chapter's recombination and wrap-up recall currently live. Chapter 1's title and label come from its hand-written book/chapters/ch01-greetings.tex, the only Latin chapter with no core/book-generation.json target.

chapters.title: Greetings
chapters.label: ch:greetings
chapters.canDo: I can greet someone in Latin, thank them, answer yes or no, and say goodbye.

payoff.summary: The whole doorway sequence on cue: salvē or avē on arrival, grātiās tibi agō, ita or nōn, and valē on the way out.

chapters.title: Numbers One to Ten
chapters.label: ch:la-numbers-one-to-ten
chapters.canDo: I can count from one to ten in Latin and say why September sits in the ninth month.

payoff.summary: Count ūnus to decem aloud, then read the Roman tally VI-X and place September against Rome's March-start year.

chapters.title: Please
chapters.label: ch:la-please
chapters.canDo: I can soften a Latin request the way Romans did, with quaesō or sīs instead of a word for please.

payoff.summary: Attach quaesō to a real request — dā mihi aquam, quaesō — and swap in sīs for the if-you-wish version.

chapters.title: Sorry
chapters.label: ch:la-sorry
chapters.canDo: I can apologise in Latin with ignōsce mihi, and use paenitet mē when I want to name the regret instead.

payoff.summary: Apologise to someone's face with ignōsce mihi, then contrast it with paenitet mē, which names regret rather than asking pardon.

chapters.title: Days of the Week
chapters.label: ch:la-days-of-the-week
chapters.canDo: I can name all seven Roman weekdays and say which modern names kept Rome's gods and which were rewritten.

payoff.summary: Name the full seven-day planetary week, then sort Saturday and Sunday by which languages kept Rome's gods and which renamed them.

chapters.title: Colours
chapters.label: ch:la-colours
chapters.canDo: I can say black, white, red, and blue in Latin, and explain why its blue was never as settled as its red.

payoff.summary: Say niger, albus, ruber, and caeruleus in turn, and split ruber's two children between French rouge and Spanish rojo.

chapters.title: Family
chapters.label: ch:la-family
chapters.canDo: I can name my father, mother, brother, and sister in Latin, and say why Spanish stopped using frāter.

payoff.summary: Name the four household members aloud, then trace frāter germānus down to Spanish hermano.

chapters.title: Head and Hand
chapters.label: ch:la-head-and-hand
chapters.canDo: I can say head and hand in Latin, and explain why manus is feminine when its declension usually is not.

payoff.summary: Say caput and manus with the correct gender, then list the manus words English still runs on.

chapters.title: Seasons
chapters.label: ch:la-seasons
chapters.canDo: I can name the four seasons in Latin and say which ones Romance rebuilt out of a phrase instead.

payoff.summary: Name vēr, aestās, autumnus, and hiems, then sort which survived plainly and which Romance rebuilt as prīma vēra and hībernum.

chapters.title: Water, Wine, and Bread
chapters.label: ch:la-water-wine-bread
chapters.canDo: I can name water, wine, and bread in Latin, and explain why a companion is someone you share bread with.

payoff.summary: Ask for aqua, vīnum, and pānis, then unpack com- plus pānis into companion.

chapters.title: Months
chapters.label: ch:la-months
chapters.canDo: I can name all twelve Roman months and say what July and August were called before they were renamed.

payoff.summary: Recite the twelve months in order, then restore Quīntīlis and Sextīlis to July and August's slots.

chapters.title: Noon and Midnight
chapters.label: ch:la-noon-and-midnight
chapters.canDo: I can say noon and midnight in Latin, and explain why English's noon does not come from either.

payoff.summary: Say medius diēs and media nox, then follow both halves into Spanish, French, and English's unrelated nōna hōra.

chapters.title: Telling Time
chapters.label: ch:la-telling-time
chapters.canDo: I can talk about the hour in Latin, and explain why a Roman hour was not a fixed sixty minutes.

payoff.summary: Say hōra, then work out how long a Roman hour actually was on a winter day against a summer one.

chapters.title: Asking Someone's Age
chapters.label: ch:la-asking-age
chapters.canDo: I can say how old I am in Latin, using the classical born-so-many-years construction.

payoff.summary: State your own age as vīgintī annōs nātus sum, and set that pattern against Romance's have-your-years and English's be-your-years.

chapters.title: Weather
chapters.label: ch:la-weather
chapters.canDo: I can say it is raining, and name heat and sun in Latin, using its subjectless weather verbs.

payoff.summary: Say pluit with no subject at all, then name calor and sol, and check the pl- to ll- path into llueve.

chapters.title: Numbers Eleven to Twenty
chapters.label: ch:la-numbers-eleven-to-twenty
chapters.canDo: I can count from eleven to twenty in Latin, including its backwards eighteen and nineteen.

payoff.summary: Count ūndecim to vīgintī aloud, then say duodēvīgintī and ūndēvīgintī and explain what they are counting backwards from.

chapters.title: Dog and Cat
chapters.label: ch:la-dog-and-cat
chapters.canDo: I can name a dog and a cat in Latin, and say which of its two cat-words came first.

payoff.summary: Name canis, fēlēs, and cattus, then say which cat-word is Classical Latin's own and where the newcomer arrived from.

chapters.title: Green and Yellow
chapters.label: ch:la-green-and-yellow
chapters.canDo: I can say green and yellow in Latin, and explain why almost no Romance language kept flāvus.

payoff.summary: Say viridis and flāvus, then follow verde one way and galbinus the other into jaune, giallo, and galben.

chapters.title: How Are You?
chapters.label: ch:la-how-are-you
chapters.canDo: I can ask someone in Latin how they are, and answer that I am well.

payoff.summary: A five-line exchange run end to end: salvē, quid agis?, valeō with grātiās tibi agō, ut valēs?, and valē from both voices.

chapters.title: Exchanging Names
chapters.label: ch:la-exchanging-names
chapters.canDo: I can ask someone's name in Latin and give my own, using the classical dative of possession.

payoff.summary: Ask quid tibi nōmen est? and answer mihi nōmen est, holding the possessor in the dative while the name itself may go either way.

chapters.title: Nice to Meet You
chapters.label: ch:la-nice-to-meet-you
chapters.canDo: I can say in Latin that it is a pleasure to have met someone, and say what that phrase really proves.

payoff.summary: Two meeting scenes: names traded with quid tibi nōmen est? between strangers, and volup est convēnisse kept for the chance re-encounter Plautus actually wrote it for.

chapters.title: You, Singular and Plural
chapters.label: ch:la-you-singular-plural
chapters.canDo: I can choose tū or vōs correctly in Latin, knowing the choice is about number and not politeness.

payoff.summary: Address one person as tū and a group as vōs, then say why neither carries politeness the way German's Sie does.

chapters.title: You're Welcome
chapters.label: ch:la-youre-welcome
chapters.canDo: I can reply to thanks in Latin with nihil est, and say honestly how classical that reply is.

payoff.summary: Answer grātiās tibi agō with nihil est, and state plainly that the reply is modern convention built from real words.

chapters.title: See You Soon
chapters.label: ch:la-see-you-soon
chapters.canDo: I can tell someone in Latin that I will see them soon, using a phrase Cicero actually wrote.

payoff.summary: Say propediem tē vidēbō as a parting line, split propediem into prope and diem, and locate it in Cicero's letters.

chapters.title: See You Tomorrow
chapters.label: ch:la-see-you-tomorrow
chapters.canDo: I can say in Latin that I will see someone tomorrow, and say which piece of it Romance mostly abandoned.

payoff.summary: Say crās tē vidēbō on the same pattern, and say honestly that this combination is not itself a surviving quotation.

chapters.title: How
chapters.label: ch:la-how
chapters.canDo: I can ask how in Latin with quōmodo, and trace it into cómo, come, and comment.

payoff.summary: Say quōmodo, split it into quō and modō, and show how comment double-marks the manner that come and cómo mark once.

chapters.title: Well
chapters.label: ch:la-well
chapters.canDo: I can answer well in Latin with bene, and show how one regular sound change turns it into bien.

payoff.summary: Answer bene when asked how you fare, then derive bien from it in one regular sound change.

chapters.title: Day
chapters.label: ch:la-day
chapters.canDo: I can use diēs on its own for day, after meeting it inside the weekday and noon phrases.

payoff.summary: Say diēs alone, point to it inside diēs Lūnae and medius diēs, and separate journal and journey from diary.

chapters.title: Night
chapters.label: ch:la-night
chapters.canDo: I can say night in Latin as nox, noctis, and see English night sitting inside it.

payoff.summary: Say nox and noctis, match it against English night, and build equinox out of aequus plus nox.

chapters.title: Good Night
chapters.label: ch:la-good-night
chapters.canDo: I can wish someone a good night in Latin, and say why the wish takes the accusative case.

payoff.summary: Wish someone bonam noctem, and say why it is not bona nox — Latin wishes take the accusative.

chapters.title: Morning
chapters.label: ch:la-morning
chapters.canDo: I can say morning in Latin with māne, and keep it apart from manus, the hand.

payoff.summary: Say māne, recover it inside dē māne and mañana, and keep long-ā mānus apart from short-a manus, the hand.

chapters.title: Good Morning
chapters.label: ch:la-good-morning
chapters.canDo: I can say good morning in Latin, and describe the salūtātiō Romans actually performed at dawn.

payoff.summary: Say bonum māne, note that its neuter case is invisible, and describe the dawn salūtātiō Romans really used.

chapters.title: Evening
chapters.label: ch:la-evening
chapters.canDo: I can say evening in Latin, and follow the vesper root into Hesperia, víspera, and vespers.

payoff.summary: Sort any European evening word into the vesper family or the sērus family, then produce vesper and the everyday vespere Cicero uses for in the evening.

chapters.title: Good Evening
chapters.label: ch:la-good-evening
chapters.canDo: I can wish someone a good evening in Latin, and point to the accusative that bonum māne could not show.

payoff.summary: Wish someone bonum vesperum, and use its masculine ending to show the accusative rule bonum māne could not.

chapters.title: Noon and Afternoon
chapters.label: ch:la-noon-and-afternoon
chapters.canDo: I can say midday in Latin, and use ante merīdiem and post merīdiem to place any hour of the day.

payoff.summary: Say merīdiēs, place an hour with ante merīdiem or post merīdiem, and say why Rome needed no separate afternoon noun.

chapters.title: Good Afternoon
chapters.label: ch:la-good-afternoon
chapters.canDo: I can greet someone in Latin in the afternoon with salvē or salvēte, and explain why nothing more is needed.

payoff.summary: One Roman day in four meetings — morning, afternoon, evening, and parting at night — with salvē and valē marked as the attested pair and the three bonus phrases marked as modern.

chapters.title: Eight Verbs at the Core
chapters.label: ch:la-core-verbs
chapters.canDo: I can say I am, I have, I go, I come, I say, I see, I know and I give in Latin, produce the he-or-she form of each, and name the English words each verb left behind.

payoff.summary: The chapter's eighth verb closes the set: after learning dō, the reader produces all eight first-person forms and all eight third-person forms in sequence — sum, habeō, eō, veniō, dīcō, videō, sciō, dō and est, habet, it, venit, dīcit, videt, scit, dat.

chapters.title: Thinking, Reading, Writing
chapters.label: ch:la-mind-verbs
chapters.canDo: I can say I think, I read, I understand and I write in Latin, produce the he-or-she form of each, and name the English words each verb built.

payoff.summary: The chapter closes on scrībō: after learning it the reader produces all four first-person forms and all four third-person forms in sequence — cōgitō, legō, intellegō, scrībō and cōgitat, legit, intellegit, scrībit.

chapters.title: Taking, Asking, Helping, Loving
chapters.label: ch:la-doing-verbs
chapters.canDo: I can say I take, I ask, I help and I love in Latin, produce the he-or-she form of each, and name the English words each verb built.

payoff.summary: The chapter closes on amō: after learning it the reader produces all four first-person forms and all four third-person forms in sequence — capiō, rogō, adiuvō, amō and capit, rogat, adiuvat, amat.

chapters.title: Hearing, Sleeping, Sitting, Standing
chapters.label: ch:la-sense-and-posture-verbs
chapters.canDo: I can say I hear, I sleep, I sit and I stand in Latin, produce the he-or-she form of each, name the conjugation each belongs to, and tell an English word inherited from the shared ancestor apart from one borrowed out of Latin.

payoff.summary: The chapter closes on stō: after learning it the reader produces all four first-person forms and all four third-person forms in sequence — audiō, dormiō, sedeō, stō and audit, dormit, sedet, stat — sorts stand from station as inherited against borrowed, and reaches back three chapters to retrieve sum and eō, neither of which had been revisited since chapter 37.

chapters.title: Walking, Running, Opening, Closing
chapters.label: ch:la-motion-verbs
chapters.canDo: I can say I walk, I run, I open and I close in Latin, produce the he-or-she form of each, name the conjugation each belongs to, and say what a Latin prefix does to the verb it sits on.

payoff.summary: The chapter closes on claudō: after learning it the reader produces all four first-person forms and all four third-person forms in sequence — ambulō, currō, aperiō, claudō and ambulat, currit, aperit, claudit — reads include/exclude beside accept/except and intellegō as one prefix rule, and so retrieves capiō and intellegō from two and three chapters back, neither of them revisited before now.

chapters.title: Bringing, Getting, Playing, Waiting
chapters.label: ch:la-getting-and-waiting-verbs
chapters.canDo: I can say I bring, I get, I play and I wait in Latin, produce the he-or-she form of each, and say whether a verb is welded together from two roots, built from a prefix on an older verb, or of ancestry nobody has settled.

payoff.summary: The chapter closes on exspectō: after learning it the reader produces all four first-person forms and all four third-person forms in sequence — ferō, accipiō, lūdō, exspectō and fert, accipit, lūdit, exspectat — sorts a verb's children from its siblings (expect against spectacle), and reaches back five chapters to retrieve videō and dō, neither of which had been revisited since chapter 37.

chapters.title: Answering, Meeting, Buying
chapters.label: ch:la-answering-meeting-buying
chapters.canDo: I can say I answer, I meet and I buy in Latin, produce the he-or-she form of each, and read an English word by recovering the older sense of the Latin verb inside it.

payoff.summary: The chapter closes on emō: after learning it the reader produces all three first-person forms and all three third-person forms in sequence — respondeō, conveniō, emō and respondet, convenit, emit — recovers redeem and example from the root's older sense 'take', and ranks the four getting-verbs capiō, accipiō, obtineō, emō against dō, retrieving capiō and dō from chapters 39 and 37.

chapters.title: The House, and Who Is Inside It
chapters.label: ch:la-domus
chapters.canDo: I can name the parts of a house in Latin — the building, its door, its wall, its garden and its hearth — and point to the English words each one left behind.

payoff.summary: The fifth word of the group, taken apart against the four before it.

chapters.title: Earth, Fire, Wind, Sky, Sea
chapters.label: ch:la-mundus
chapters.canDo: I can name the five great outdoor things in Latin and say which of them English inherited by descent and which it borrowed from books.

payoff.summary: The fifth word of the group, taken apart against the four before it.

chapters.title: Light, Shadow, and Going to Sleep
chapters.label: ch:la-lux
chapters.canDo: I can name light, shadow, star, moon and sleep in Latin, and use them to close a day the way a Latin speaker would.

payoff.summary: The fifth word of the group, taken apart against the four before it.

chapters.title: Salt, Honey, Milk, Egg, Fish
chapters.label: ch:la-mensa
chapters.canDo: I can name five things on a Latin table, and I can use Grimm's Law to tell an inherited English cousin from a borrowed Latin loan.

payoff.summary: The fifth word of the group, taken apart against the four before it.
